guides.title: The city of fifty-two towers
guides.text:
Before you rise the ramparts of Carcassonne. Fifty-two towers, three kilometres of walls, two thousand years of history.

In twelve hundred and nine, the crusade against the Cathars sweeps across this land. The city is besieged in the height of summer. Cut off from water, it falls in fifteen days. Its young viscount, Raymond-Roger Trencavel, only twenty-four years old, is thrown into a dungeon of his own castle. He dies there three months later. Officially, of dysentery. Many whispered: murdered.

Walk along the lices, between the Gallo-Roman and the medieval walls. Every stone has watched the crusaders of Simon de Montfort pass by, the builders of Saint Louis, and seven centuries of garrisons.

In the nineteenth century, the city lay in ruins. One man, Viollet-le-Duc, brought it back to life. To him we owe these controversial slate roofs, and this dream of stone, now a World Heritage site.

Listen to the wind in the battlements. Here, memory has never fallen silent.

guides.title: The last pyre
guides.text:
Twelve hundred metres of climbing, and the sanctuary appears: Montségur. The rocky peak rises like the prow of a ship above the mists of the Ariège. It was here that Catharism fought its last great battle.

Ten months of siege. Six thousand men below, a handful of defenders above. In March, twelve hundred and forty-four, the fortress surrenders. Those who recant are offered their lives.

Two hundred and five men and women refuse. They walk down the mountain singing, and climb of their own will onto the pyre built in the meadow you see below. The prat dels cremats. The field of the burned.

But the legend does not end there. The night before the surrender, four Cathar perfects are said to have escaped into the darkness, carrying the Cathar treasure. Gold? Manuscripts? The Grail itself, as some claim? No one has ever found it.

Look to the horizon from these ruins. Perhaps it is still there, somewhere, beneath your feet.

guides.title: The celestial Carcassonne
guides.text:
Eight hundred metres above sea level. A ridge of white limestone, three hundred metres long. And a castle that seems born from the rock itself: Peyrepertuse, the pierced stone.

They call it the celestial Carcassonne. It is the largest of the vertigo citadels, those royal fortresses that guarded the border between France and Aragon.

Climb the Saint Louis staircase, carved into the cliff face. In high wind, you cling to it with both hands. Below, the Corbières unfold their vineyards and scrubland all the way to the sea. On a clear day, you can glimpse the Mediterranean.

During the crusade, the lord of Peyrepertuse sheltered hunted Cathars. Excommunicated and pursued, he finally submitted in twelve hundred and forty. The castle then became a sentinel of the King of France, facing the kingdom of Aragon, for four centuries.

When the Treaty of the Pyrenees moved the border in sixteen fifty-nine, the citadel lost its purpose. It fell asleep. It was waiting for you.

guides.title: The last refuge
guides.text:
A finger of stone pointing to the sky, visible for tens of kilometres: Quéribus, the last refuge.

The year is twelve hundred and fifty-five. Montségur fell eleven years earlier. Everywhere, the Inquisition hunts the last perfects. It is here, in this eagle's nest seven hundred and twenty-eight metres high, that the final Cathars take shelter, around the deacon Benoît de Termes.

King Saint Louis sends an army. The castle surrenders without a fight. But the Cathars have already vanished into the mountains, toward Spain. No pyre at Quéribus. Only a silent disappearance.

Climb into the polygonal keep. The hall of the pillar awaits you: a single column that blossoms into a Gothic palm tree of stone. Through the arrow slit, your gaze plunges over a thousand metres of emptiness, all the way to the vineyards of Roussillon and the blue line of the Mediterranean.

Here ends the military history of Catharism. Here begins its legend.

guides.title: The memory of water and fire
guides.text:
An island of stone between two gorges carved by rivers. A natural bridge hollowed out by the waters. Minerve, one of the most beautiful villages of France, and one of the most tragic.

Summer, twelve hundred and ten. Simon de Montfort besieges the town, which shelters a hundred and forty Cathar perfects who fled after the massacre of Béziers. His war machine, the Malvoisine, the bad neighbour, pounds the village's only well. Without water, under the July sun, Minerve surrenders after five weeks.

The perfects are offered their lives in exchange for recantation. A hundred and forty refuse. They are cast into the first great collective pyre of the crusade. Some, the chronicle says, threw themselves in.

Today, walk down the Street of the Martyrs. A dove of stone watches over the square. It is engraved with a single Occitan word. Als catars. To the Cathars.

Beneath your feet, the tunnels of the Brian river. Above, the silence of the Minervois. And everywhere, the memory of water and fire.

guides.title: The secret of Abbé Saunière
guides.text:
A village of fewer than a hundred souls, perched on its hill in the Aude. And yet, the whole world knows its name: Rennes-le-Château.

Eighteen eighty-five. A young priest, Bérenger Saunière, takes charge of the parish. He is poor. The church is falling apart. Then, in just a few years, everything changes. Saunière spends fortunes. He renovates the church in a strange, flamboyant style, and has carved above the door: this place is terrible.

Where does the money come from? Trafficking in masses, answers the Church, which suspends him. Treasure, answers the legend: parchments found in a Visigothic pillar, the gold of the Templars, or a secret capable of shaking Rome itself.

Saunière dies in nineteen seventeen without ever speaking. His housekeeper once promised to reveal a secret that grants power. She too died in silence.

Look at the devil holding the holy water font, the stations of the cross with their unexplained details. Here, every stone is a riddle. And the riddle is still unsolved.

guides.title: The challenge of Rome's engineers
guides.text:
Three tiers of golden arches span the Gardon river. Forty-nine metres high. The Pont du Gard, the tallest aqueduct bridge Rome ever built.

In the first century, it was only one link in a prodigious work: fifty kilometres of channel to carry water all the way to Nîmes. Over that whole distance, the average slope is twenty-five centimetres per kilometre. A precision that still challenges our engineers today.

Look at the stones. Some weigh six tonnes, hoisted by hand, without mortar, fitted to the millimetre. On the blocks, the marks carved by the workers to guide the assembly are still legible.

For five centuries, water flowed up there, layer of limestone after layer of limestone. Then Rome faded, and the aqueduct fell silent.

But the bridge remained standing. Two thousand years later, it still lifts toward the sky the quiet pride of the builders of the Empire.

guides.title: The arena that never died
guides.text:
A hundred and thirty-three metres long, two tiers of arcades, twenty-four thousand spectators. This is the arena of Nîmes, the best-preserved Roman amphitheatre in the world.

At the end of the first century, the crowd packs in for the gladiator fights. A system of corridors and vomitoria could empty the building in minutes. Rome already thought like an engineer of crowds.

Then the Empire falls. And the arena does not die: it transforms. The Visigoths turn it into a fortress. In the Middle Ages, a whole village settles in its tiers: two hundred houses, two chapels, crammed into the Roman stone.

In the nineteenth century, the amphitheatre is finally cleared of its inhabitants and given back to spectacle.

Even today, bullfights, concerts and reenactments echo beneath these vaults. Two thousand years of roaring crowds, without a single generation of silence.

guides.title: The sacred rock of Athena
guides.text:
Above Athens, on a rock of limestone, rises the very symbol of Greek civilisation: the Acropolis.

The year is four hundred and forty-seven before our era. Athens is at the height of its glory. Under the authority of Pericles, the sculptor Phidias and the architects Ictinus and Callicrates raise the Parthenon, temple of the goddess Athena. It will be built in less than fifteen years.

Look at its columns. None is truly straight: they swell slightly, they lean imperceptibly inward. Optical corrections, calculated so that the eye sees them as perfect. Geometry in the service of illusion.

The temple was a church, then a mosque, then a powder magazine. In sixteen eighty-seven, a Venetian shell blew it apart. What you see is a survivor.

And yet, two thousand five hundred years later, it still holds up the sky of Attica. Here, beauty has outlasted everything.

guides.title: The theatre of blood and power
guides.text:
Fifty thousand spectators. Four storeys. A façade of travertine as tall as a fifteen-storey building. The Colosseum, the largest amphitheatre ever built.

Inaugurated in the year eighty by the emperor Titus, it was celebrated with a hundred days of games. Gladiator fights, hunts of wild beasts, and, it is said, naval battles in a flooded arena.

Beneath the wooden floor covered in sand lay a labyrinth of galleries, the hypogeum: cages, hoists, trapdoors from which lions and warriors would suddenly appear. A theatre machine in the service of death.

Its very name comes from a nearby colossus: a bronze statue thirty metres tall, in the likeness of Nero, that once stood close by.

Earthquakes, looting and centuries of neglect have half-ruined it. But it still dominates Rome, a monument to the grandeur, and the cruelty, of an empire that made a spectacle of death.

guides.title: The lost city of the Incas
guides.text:
At two thousand four hundred metres, between two dizzying peaks, a city of stone rises from the clouds: Machu Picchu.

Built around fourteen fifty for the Inca emperor Pachacutec, it gathers temples, terraces and palaces, assembled without mortar, without the wheel, without a single tool of iron. The blocks fit so perfectly that no blade slips between them, and they have resisted earthquakes for five centuries.

Less than a century after it was built, the Incas abandoned it. The Spanish conquest ravaged the empire, but the conquistadors never found the city. The jungle covered it, and the world forgot it.

In nineteen eleven, an American explorer, guided by a local child, pushed aside the vines and rediscovered it almost intact.

At sunrise, on the equinox, a ray of light crosses a window of the Temple of the Sun and strikes a sacred stone. The Incas had built their city to speak with the sky.

guides.title: The rose-red city carved in rock
guides.text:
You move forward through the Siq, a narrow crack between two walls a hundred metres high. You walk for several minutes in the shadows. And suddenly, in the gap of the rock, a rose-coloured façade blazes in the sun: the Treasury. You have reached Petra.

More than two thousand years ago, the Nabataeans, a people of caravan traders, made this desert a crossroads of the world. Frankincense from Arabia, silk from China, spices from India passed through their hands. From it they drew an immense fortune.

From this wealth, they carved a city into the very cliff: temples, tombs, a theatre seating three thousand. And a hidden genius: an entire network of channels and cisterns to capture the smallest drop of water in the heart of the desert.

Then the trade routes shifted. Petra declined, an earthquake broke it, and for centuries only the Bedouin knew its secret.

In eighteen twelve, a Swiss traveller in disguise revealed it to the world. The rose-red city, forgotten, had been waiting for its hour.

guides.title: The temple-mountain of the gods
guides.text:
At daybreak, its five towers, shaped like lotus buds, are mirrored in the pools. Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument in the world.

In the twelfth century, the Khmer king Suryavarman the Second ordered its construction. Tens of thousands of workers, five million tonnes of sandstone carried from a distant quarry, and three decades of labour. The temple is conceived as an image of the universe: its towers represent the five peaks of Mount Meru, home of the gods, and its moat, the primordial ocean.

Over nearly eight hundred metres, bas-reliefs unfold armies, gods and demons churning the sea of milk to draw from it the elixir of immortality.

Hindu at first, the temple later became Buddhist. It was never fully abandoned: monks have always prayed here.

Its silhouette now adorns the flag of Cambodia. A whole people recognises itself in this mountain of stone offered to the gods.

guides.title: The wonder of the West
guides.text:
Between sky and sea, a pyramid of granite rises from the sands: Mont-Saint-Michel, crowned by its abbey.

It all begins in the year seven hundred and eight. The archangel Michael appears in a dream to the bishop of Avranches and orders him to build a sanctuary on this rock. First a simple oratory; then, century after century, an abbey that climbs to storm the summit.

In the thirteenth century, they raise the Marvel: three levels of Gothic halls stacked on the cliff, a hanging cloister, a refectory bathed in light. A challenge thrown at gravity.

Around it, the bay has the greatest tides in Europe. The sea, they say, rises there at the speed of a galloping horse, surrounding the Mount and making it, twice a day, almost impossible to reach.

A fortress never taken during the Hundred Years' War, a prison under the Revolution, the Mount is today one of the most visited sites in France. A rock where mankind tried to touch the sky.

guides.title: When Avignon ruled Christendom
guides.text:
Fifteen thousand square metres of stone, towers fifty metres high, walls several metres thick: the Palace of the Popes, the largest Gothic palace in the world.

In the fourteenth century, the unthinkable happens: the papacy leaves Rome for Avignon. For nearly seventy years, nine popes follow one another here, and the little Provençal town becomes the capital of Western Christendom.

In less than twenty years, two builder-popes raise this fortress. Behind these austere walls hid an unheard-of luxury, brilliant frescoes, treasures, and one of the most dazzling courts in Europe.

Then the popes return to Rome, and the Great Schism tears the Church apart: two rival popes, one in Rome, the other here, excommunicating each other.

Under the Revolution, the palace became a barracks and a prison; the soldiers scraped the frescoes. Enough remains to imagine the lost splendour. Here, for a time, all of Europe revolved around Avignon.

guides.title: The last wonder of the world
guides.text:
On the Giza plateau, at the edge of the desert, three mountains of stone have defied time for forty-five centuries: the pyramids.

The greatest, that of Khufu, once rose a hundred and forty-six metres. For nearly four thousand years, it was the tallest human structure on the planet. Two million three hundred thousand blocks, weighing on average two and a half tonnes, assembled with a precision that still troubles engineers.

The faces are aligned with the four cardinal points with near-perfect accuracy. How, without a compass? The mystery remains.

It was built not by slaves, as long believed, but by workers who were housed, fed and paid, whose villages and tombs have been found.

Of the seven wonders of the ancient world, the pyramids are the only ones still standing. The pharaohs wanted eternity. Under this unchanging sky, it seems they obtained it.

guides.title: The city frozen by Vesuvius
guides.text:
In the year seventy-nine, the city of Pompeii lives an ordinary day under the sun of the Bay of Naples. Twenty thousand inhabitants, paved streets, baths, theatres, a bustling forum.

Then Vesuvius awakens. In a few hours, a column of ash rises thirty kilometres into the sky. The city is buried under several metres of pumice and burning ash. Those who did not flee are caught where they stand.

And Pompeii vanishes. For more than fifteen hundred years, even its location is forgotten.

When the excavations reveal it, the world discovers a time capsule: frescoes with intact colours, bread still in the ovens, graffiti on the walls. And, in the hardened ash, the hollow left by vanished bodies, which was filled with plaster to recover, frozen forever, the final gestures of the victims.

To walk through Pompeii is to walk through a single day, two thousand years ago, cut short in an instant.

guides.title: The city of three cultures
guides.text:
On a spur of rock that the Tagus almost entirely embraces, stands Toledo, the former capital of Spain. They call it the city of three cultures.

For centuries, Christians, Muslims and Jews lived side by side here. From that meeting was born an intellectual miracle: the school of translators. Here, Greek, Arabic and Hebrew knowledge passed into Latin, and Europe rediscovered Aristotle, medicine, astronomy, algebra. Part of our science was born in these alleyways.

Walk through the old town: an immense Gothic cathedral, synagogues turned into churches, a thousand-year-old mosque, all touching and answering one another in a maze of stone.

In the sixteenth century, the painter El Greco made Toledo his city. His stormy skies above the town are among the most famous in all painting.

Now frozen in its setting of golden stone, Toledo keeps the memory of a time when three worlds, here, spoke to one another.

guides.title: The plunder of Constantinople
guides.text:
A city set upon the water, built on millions of wooden piles driven into the lagoon. Venice, the Serenissima, which ruled the Mediterranean for a thousand years.

At the heart of Saint Mark's Square, the basilica glitters with golden domes and Byzantine mosaics. It holds one of the most fabulous treasures in Europe.

Its origin? A plunder. In twelve hundred and four, the Venetian crusaders, instead of marching on Jerusalem, sacked Constantinople, the richest Christian city. They brought back heaps of gold, relics and jewels.

From this loot, admire the Pala d'Oro, an altarpiece of gold set with thousands of pearls and enamels, and the four ancient bronze horses that once adorned the hippodrome of Constantinople.

Doges, merchants and spies shaped this power born of water and trade. Venice had neither land nor mines. Its fortune, it took from the sea, and from others.

guides.title: The stone dream of Francis the First
guides.text:
In the heart of the Sologne, surrounded by the largest enclosed park in Europe, rises a mirage: Chambord, the greatest château of the French Renaissance.

In fifteen nineteen, a king of twenty-five, Francis the First, launches its construction. Four hundred and forty rooms, three hundred and sixty chimneys, a forest of towers and dormers that seems to have stepped out of a fairy tale.

At its centre, the double-helix staircase: two flights coiled around each other, so that one can climb and descend without ever meeting. It is whispered that Leonardo da Vinci, guest of the king and dead nearby a few months earlier, inspired its design.

And yet, Francis the First stayed here only a few weeks in his entire life. The château, half-furnished, long remained a stage set more than a home.

The stone dream of a king who wanted to dazzle the world, Chambord had, at heart, only one purpose: to proclaim his glory. In that, it succeeded magnificently.
